title: Meeting Environmental Challenges: The Role of Human Identity

findings.consequent: negative attitudes towards non-human nature (viewing humans as consumers of nature)
findings.mechanism: Values influence higher-order cognitions that shape attitudes towards the world.
findings.quote: people who strongly endorse such self-enhancing, materialistic values also express more negative attitudes towards non-human nature.

findings.antecedent: stronger values placed on power and achievement
findings.consequent: less concern about how environmental damage affects other humans, children, future generations and non-human life
findings.mechanism: Values influence higher-order cognitions that shape concern for others and the environment.
findings.quote: stronger values placed on power and achievement are associated with less concern about how environmental damage affects other humans, children, future generations and non-human life.

findings.consequent: less positive attitudes towards the environment and lower levels of biophilia
findings.mechanism: Materialistic goals are in conflict with values that promote affiliation with life.
findings.quote: caring more about such goals is associated with significantly less positive attitudes towards the environ-ment, and with lower levels of biophilia

findings.antecedent: stronger endorsement of materialistic goals in life (adolescents)
findings.consequent: less likely to engage in positive environmental behaviours (e.g., turning off lights, recycling, reusing paper)
findings.mechanism: Materialistic goals organize lower-level behaviors, making pro-environmental actions less likely.
findings.quote: adolescents who more strongly endorse materialistic goals in life report themselves as being less likely to turn off lights in unused rooms, to recycle, to reuse paper and to engage in other positive environmental behaviours

findings.consequent: negatively correlated with the frequency of engagement in pro-environmental behaviours (e.g., riding a bicycle, reusing paper, buying second-hand, recycling)
findings.mechanism: Materialistic values organize lower-level behaviors, making pro-environmental actions less likely.
findings.quote: materialistic values are found to be negatively correlated with the frequency of engagement in pro-environmental behaviours

findings.antecedent: high focus on materialistic goals (North American adults)
findings.consequent: higher ecological footprint arising from lifestyle choices regarding transportation, housing and diet
findings.mechanism: Materialistic goals influence lifestyle choices that have environmental impacts.
findings.quote: A relatively high focus on materialistic goals related to a higher ecological footprint arising from lifestyle choices regarding transportation, housing and diet.

findings.antecedent: group composed of individuals with relatively highly materialistic goals (forest-management game)
findings.consequent: exploited forest resources more intensively and were significantly less likely to have any trees remaining at 25th year of bidding
findings.mechanism: Materialistic goals lead to more exploitative resource management behaviors.
findings.quote: those composed of four individuals who all scored relatively highly in materialistic goals exploited the forest resources more intensively, and were significantly less likely to have any trees remaining at the 25th year of bidding.

findings.antecedent: citizens placed a greater priority on pursuing goals such as wealth, achievement and status (materialistic values) in 20 wealthy nations
findings.consequent: higher per capita CO2 emissions (after controlling for GDP)
findings.mechanism: National prioritization of materialistic values influences collective environmental behavior.
findings.quote: per capita CO2 emissions were higher in countries where citizens placed a greater priority on pursuing goals such as wealth, achievement and status.

findings.consequent: strongly correlated with environmental attitudes and behaviours
findings.mechanism: A sense of connection to nature fosters pro-environmental attitudes and behaviors.
findings.source: text, p.21 (Frantz et al., 2005; Mayer & Frantz, 2004; Schultz, 2001)
findings.quote: connectedness is strongly correlated with environmental attitudes and behaviours

findings.consequent: one of the strongest and most consistent motivational predictors of pro-environmental behaviour
findings.mechanism: Environmental identity provides motivation for pro-environmental actions.
findings.quote: connectedness with nature emerged as one of the strongest and most consistent motivational predictors of pro-environmental behaviour

findings.consequent: used to describe socially unacceptable people
findings.mechanism: Semantic associations reflect underlying social categorization and prejudice.
findings.quote: a remarkable number of the nouns used to describe socially unacceptable people were ani-mal words

findings.consequent: more likely to be attributed uniquely human, secondary emotions (e.g., remorse, affection, pride, conceit) than out-group members
findings.mechanism: Social categorization leads to infrahumanization of out-groups, denying them full human emotional capacity.
findings.quote: members of their in-group are more likely to experience these uniquely human, secondary emotions than are members of the out-group.

findings.consequent: significantly more likely to be associated with human words than with foreign names
findings.mechanism: In-group favoritism and out-group derogation manifest in word associations.
findings.quote: British participants were significantly more likely to associate human words with British names than with foreign names

findings.consequent: significantly more likely to be associated with animal words than with British names
findings.mechanism: Out-group derogation links foreign groups to less human (animal) characteristics.
findings.quote: significantly more likely to associate animal words with foreign names than with British names.

findings.antecedent: ascribing greater rights to individual animals
findings.consequent: more positive orientations toward the environment
findings.mechanism: Recognizing rights of individual animals extends to a broader positive orientation towards the environment.
findings.quote: those who ascribe greater rights to individual animals also express more positive orientations toward the environment.

findings.antecedent: thoughts of global warming creating feelings of fear or helplessness (small-town Norwegians)
findings.consequent: limit their exposure to information which may create anxiety (e.g., avoiding reading details, reluctance to engage in conversation)
findings.mechanism: Emotional management strategy of selective attention to avoid unpleasant feelings.
findings.quote: her respondents would limit their exposure to information which may create anxiety.

findings.antecedent: awareness about future impacts of climate change (potential anxiety)
findings.consequent: keeping one's thoughts in the present (avoidance)
findings.mechanism: Emotional management strategy of selective attention to avoid future-oriented anxiety.
findings.quote: keeping one's thoughts in the present, so that awareness about future impacts of climate change is avoided.

findings.consequent: doing something, however small (e.g., turning down thermostat, turning off water) to displace feeling
findings.mechanism: Displaced commitment as a coping strategy to manage feelings of hopelessness.
findings.quote: By turning down the thermostat a few degrees, or turning off the water whilst brushing their teeth, people can at least temporarily displace their feeling of hopelessness by taking action.

findings.consequent: seeking pleasure (pursuing exciting experiences/possessions) as a coping strategy
findings.mechanism: Diversion strategy to provide psychic relief from anxiety related to environmental problems.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found that ‘seeking pleasure' was the strategy most highly endorsed across three samples of adults.

findings.antecedent: extent of using 'seeking pleasure' coping strategy
findings.consequent: lower level of reported stress from awareness of environmental problems
findings.mechanism: Seeking pleasure provides psychic relief, reducing reported stress.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found a negative association between the extent to which people reported using this strategy and the level of stress they reported as arising from an awareness of environmental problems.

findings.consequent: positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Diversion strategies do not translate into pro-environmental action.
findings.quote: seeking pleasure did not motivate positive environmental behaviours, and in some samples this strategy was actually associated with less engagement in such beneficial behaviours.

findings.antecedent: using 'relativisation' coping strategy (claiming environmental problems are not so great)
findings.consequent: lower levels of stress from environmental damage
findings.mechanism: Reinterpreting threats reduces their perceived severity and associated stress.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found that this strategy was consistently associated with lower levels of stress from environmental damage

findings.consequent: greater pro-environmental behaviour
findings.mechanism: Reinterpretive coping strategies do not translate into pro-environmental action.
findings.quote: endorsing relativisation did not promote greater pro-environmental behaviour.

findings.antecedent: deploying 'denial of guilt' coping strategy (claiming environmental damage is not one's fault)
findings.consequent: lower levels of stress from environmental problems
findings.mechanism: Denial reduces personal responsibility and associated stress.
findings.source: text, p.27 (Homburg et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann et al., 2001; Norgaard, 2006)
findings.quote: denial of guilt helps lower levels of stress from environmental problems but did not propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.consequent: propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Denial of guilt does not motivate pro-environmental action.
findings.source: text, p.27 (Homburg et al., 2007; Stoll-Kleemann et al., 2001; Norgaard, 2006)
findings.quote: denial of guilt helps lower levels of stress from environmental problems but did not propel people to engage in positive environmental behaviours.

findings.consequent: projection (blaming other individuals or groups, e.g., 'Amerika')
findings.mechanism: Projection is a defense mechanism to manage guilt by externalizing blame.
findings.quote: Norgaard found substantial evidence for this form of emotion management, as many of her Norwegian respondents repeatedly identified “Amerika” as the real source of ecological problems.

findings.antecedent: using 'resignation' coping strategy (accepting environmental problems as inevitable)
findings.consequent: significantly less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Apathy and resignation lead to inaction regarding environmental problems.
findings.quote: people were significantly less likely to engage in pro-environmental behaviours to the extent that they used the strategy of resignation

findings.antecedent: briefly reminded of one's own death (writing essays)
findings.consequent: attached greater importance to money, image and status (materialistic values)
findings.mechanism: Terror management theory: mortality salience leads to self-esteem enhancement through cultural values like materialism.
findings.quote: subjects randomly as-signed to write short essays about their own death attached greater importance to money, image and status

findings.consequent: reported being more excited at the prospect of finding $20
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases the appeal of material rewards as a means of self-esteem enhancement.
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death reported being more excited at the prospect of finding $20

findings.consequent: more attracted to high-status goods (e.g., Lexus car, Rolex watch), but not low-status goods (e.g., Geo-Metro car, Pringles)
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases the appeal of status-enhancing material possessions.
findings.quote: after having mortality made salient, subjects were more attracted to goods such as a Lexus car or a Rolex watch

findings.consequent: increased expectations about future financial worth and expected spending on clothing, entertainment, leisure activities
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience drives a compensatory striving for material success and consumption.
findings.quote: Writing about their own death has also been found to increase undergraduates' expectations about their future financial worth, as well as how much they expect to spend on clothing, entertainment and leisure activities

findings.consequent: leads judges to assign harsher punishments to prostitutes, Americans to provide greater monetary rewards to those who uphold common cultural values, and college students to be more antagonistic towards out-group members
findings.mechanism: Terror management theory: mortality salience increases in-group favoritism and out-group derogation to bolster cultural worldviews.
findings.quote: thinking about death leads judges to assign harsher punishments to prostitutes, Americans to provide greater monetary rewards to those who uphold common cultural values, and college students to be more antagonistic towards out-group members

findings.consequent: became especially disgusted by animals (e.g., maggots, cockroaches) and body products
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases disgust towards aspects of existence that remind humans of their animal nature.
findings.quote: subjects who had written about their own death became especially disgusted by animals (seeing maggots or cockroaches) and body products

findings.antecedent: written about their own death AND read essay proclaiming similarities between animals and humans
findings.consequent: rated the author of the essay as less likable, intelligent, and knowledgeable
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience leads to derogation of those who challenge human uniqueness from animals.
findings.quote: the subjects who had written about their own death rated the author of the essay proclaiming the similarities between animals and humans as less likable, intelligent, and knowledgeable

findings.consequent: express more negative attitudes towards aspects of human behaviour shared with animals (e.g., breastfeeding, sex) and towards animals in general
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience increases efforts to distance humans from their animal nature.
findings.source: text, p.30 (Goldenberg et al., 2006; Beatson & Halloran, 2007)
findings.quote: thoughts of death can cause people to express more negative attitudes towards those as-pects of human behaviour that are shared with animals... and towards animals in general

findings.consequent: significantly more likely to report thinking about death than when in cultivated nature or the city
findings.mechanism: Wild nature, being untamed, can evoke existential fears and reminders of mortality.
findings.quote: subjects were significantly more likely to report that they thought about death when they were in wild nature

findings.consequent: view cultivated, humanised nature as more beautiful and rate wild, untamed nature as less beautiful
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience leads to preference for tamed, controlled environments over wild, untamed ones.
findings.quote: Reminders of death... were also found by these researchers to cause subjects to view cultivated, humanised nature as more beautiful and to rate wild, untamed nature as less beautiful.

findings.antecedent: writing brief essays about their own death
findings.consequent: made bids to cut down significantly more acres of forest in a simulated forest-management game
findings.mechanism: Mortality salience stimulates a tendency to transform or destroy wilderness.
findings.quote: Subjects who had written about death made bids to cut down significantly more acres of forest.

findings.antecedent: exposing people to messages promoting materialistic values (social modelling, media, competitive context)
findings.consequent: tend to adopt such values themselves / express materialistic values more strongly
findings.mechanism: Social learning and cultural context shape individual values.
findings.quote: exposing people to messages promoting materialistic values tends to lead them to adopt such values themselves.

findings.antecedent: psychological insecurity (death reminders, cold/controlling parents, divorce, economic deprivation, temporary hunger)
findings.consequent: orientation towards materialistic values
findings.mechanism: Insecurity drives compensatory striving for material possessions and status.
findings.quote: Psychological insecurity is the second factor known to cause an orientation towards materialistic values.

findings.antecedent: greater priority on intrinsic/self-transcendent values (self-acceptance/self-direction, affiliation/benevolence, community feeling/universalism)
findings.consequent: oppose environmentally damaging self-enhancing/materialistic values and promote more positive environmental attitudes and sustainable lifestyles
findings.mechanism: Intrinsic and self-transcendent values are psychologically antagonistic to materialistic values and align with pro-environmental outcomes.
findings.quote: such values both oppose environmentally damaging self-enhancing and materialistic values and promote more positive environmental attitudes and sustainable lifestyles

findings.antecedent: reading task framed as relevant to intrinsic goal of benefiting the community
findings.consequent: learned the material in the text more deeply and were more likely to voluntarily visit the library and a recycling plant to learn more about recycling
findings.mechanism: Intrinsic motivation enhances engagement and learning, leading to pro-environmental actions.
findings.quote: those who had the goal framed in intrinsic terms not only learned the material in the text more deeply, but were also more likely to voluntarily visit the library and a recycling plant to learn more about recycling.

findings.antecedent: chosen to ‘downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle
findings.consequent: live in more ecologically sustainable ways than mainstream Americans
findings.mechanism: Lifestyle choices driven by intrinsic values lead to reduced ecological footprint.
findings.quote: those who have chosen to ‘downshift' or pursue a 'voluntarily simple' lifestyle also live in more ecologically sustainable ways

findings.consequent: effective in increasing compliance with speed limits, decreasing amount people drive, increasing use of public transportation and stores selling sustainable products
findings.mechanism: Implementation intentions automatize behavior, reducing cognitive effort for goal-consistent actions.
findings.source: text, p.45 (Elliott & Armitage, 2006; Eriksson et al., 2008; Bamberg, 2002)
findings.quote: implementation intentions have been effective in in-creasing compliance with speed limits... in decreasing the amount people drive... and in increasing people's use of both public transportation and stores that sell sustainable products.

findings.antecedent: higher levels of Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) (college students)
findings.consequent: significantly more likely to endorse and personally use “products made by injuring or killing animals”
findings.mechanism: SDO reflects a desire for group dominance, extending to exploitation of non-human nature.
findings.quote: college students displaying higher levels of SDO are sig-nificantly more likely to endorse and personally use “products made by injuring or killing animals”

findings.consequent: most frequent justification given by participants was 'necessity'
findings.mechanism: Legitimizing myths are used to justify behaviors that exploit animals.
findings.quote: The most frequent justification that participants in her study gave for using animals was "necessity”.

findings.consequent: low in materialistic values and high in intrinsic values
findings.mechanism: Empathy fosters other-oriented values, conflicting with self-enhancing materialism.
findings.quote: People high in empathy tend to be low in materialistic values and high in intrinsic values

findings.consequent: lower levels of prejudice across a number of different types of out-groups
findings.mechanism: Empathy promotes understanding and reduces negative attitudes towards out-groups.
findings.quote: They also tend to display lower levels of prejudice across a number of different types of out-groups

findings.antecedent: value confrontation (feedback on discrepancies between egalitarian values and behavior/peers)
findings.consequent: effective for individuals who endorse egalitarian values but still hold prejudicial attitudes towards out-groups (reduction in prejudice)
findings.mechanism: Creating cognitive dissonance motivates individuals to align their values and behaviors, reducing prejudice.
findings.quote: recent re-search suggests it can be quite effective for individuals who endorse egalitarian values but nonetheless still hold some prejudicial attitudes towards out-groups

findings.antecedent: perspective-taking intervention ('try to feel the full impact' of someone's experience)
findings.consequent: increases empathy for groups and declines in prejudice towards these individuals
findings.mechanism: Perspective-taking fosters empathy, which reduces prejudice.
findings.source: text, p.52 (Batson et al., 2002; Whitley & Kite, 2006)
findings.quote: this relatively simple intervention increases empathy for groups as diverse as drug dealers, older people, African Americans, AIDS patients and the homeless, with consequent declines in prejudice towards these individuals

findings.antecedent: asked to take animals' perspective (viewing pictures of harmed animals)
findings.consequent: express significantly higher levels of biospheric environmental concern (concern for all living things)
findings.mechanism: Perspective-taking generates empathy, leading to greater concern for non-human nature.
findings.quote: Subjects who were asked to take the animals' perspective were found to express significantly higher levels of biospheric environmental concern

findings.antecedent: reporting unpleasant emotions such as anger and sadness in response to environmental stresses
findings.consequent: more likely to engage in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Unpleasant emotions can motivate action when processed constructively.
findings.quote: those subjects who report unpleasant emotions such as anger and sadness in response to environmental stresses are more likely to engage in posi-tive environmental behaviours.

findings.antecedent: sustained, reflective meditation on the feelings aroused by thoughts of death
findings.consequent: decrease materialistic strivings
findings.mechanism: Sustained reflection on mortality can lead to a shift towards self-transcendent and intrinsic values, reducing materialism.
findings.source: text, p.58 (Cozzolino et al., 2004; Lykins et al., 2007)
findings.quote: a more sustained, reflective meditation on the feelings aroused by thoughts of death can actually decrease materialistic strivings

findings.antecedent: mortality salience (fear of death) AND thinking about the possibility of an afterlife (alternative coping)
findings.consequent: disappearance of the effect of mortality salience on unsustainable resource use
findings.mechanism: Alternative coping mechanisms can buffer the negative effects of mortality salience.
findings.quote: this effect disappeared when people were provided with an alternative means of coping with the fear of their own death: in this case, thinking about the possibility of an afterlife.

findings.antecedent: endorsing problem-solving coping strategy (seeking information, educating oneself, social support)
findings.consequent: one of the best predictors of engaging in positive environmental behaviours
findings.mechanism: Active engagement with problems and seeking solutions directly leads to positive behaviors.
findings.quote: one of the best predictors of engaging in positive environmental behaviours was endorsing this problem-solving coping strategy.

findings.consequent: increased levels of reported stress from an awareness of environmental challenges
findings.mechanism: Directly confronting environmental problems can increase stress, even if leading to action.
findings.quote: Homburg and colleagues found problem-solving strategies to be associated with increased levels of reported stress from an awareness of environmental challenges.

findings.consequent: reduced desire for materialistic attainments, less likely to endorse materialistic values, and more likely to endorse intrinsic values
findings.mechanism: Mindfulness promotes acceptance of present experience, reducing compensatory materialistic strivings.
findings.source: text, p.60 (Brown et al., 2009; Brown & Kasser, 2005)
findings.quote: mindfulness was associated with reduced desire for materialistic attainments, and Brown and Kasser (2005) found that more mindful people were less likely to endorse materialistic values and more likely to endorse intrinsic values.

findings.consequent: engaged in more positive environmental behaviours and had lower ecological footprints
findings.mechanism: Mindfulness fosters greater awareness and acceptance, leading to more sustainable behaviors.
findings.quote: adults who were more mindful engaged in more positive environmental behaviours and had lower ecological footprints

findings.consequent: extent to which people endorse materialistic values
findings.mechanism: Materialistic values are primarily shaped by social experiences, not genetics.
findings.source: text, p.67 (Giddens et al., 2009; Kasser et al., 2004)
findings.quote: the extent to which people endorse materialistic values seems to have little to do with genetics

findings.consequent: evaluations attached to categorizations (prejudice)
findings.mechanism: While categorization may be innate, the evaluative content of prejudice is learned.
findings.quote: the evaluations they attach to those categorisations are largely learned

findings.consequent: means by which people cope with threat
findings.mechanism: Cultural norms and messages shape acceptable and common coping strategies.
findings.quote: the means by which people cope with threat is largely shaped by messages received from their culture

findings.consequent: less concern for social justice, equality, and a world at peace, less pro-social behaviour, and more manipulative, competitive behaviour
findings.mechanism: Materialistic values prioritize self-interest, conflicting with broader social and environmental concerns.
findings.quote: self-enhancing, materialistic values are not only associated with more negative environmental attitudes and behaviours, but also with less concern for social justice, equality, and a world at peace, less pro-social behaviour, and more manipulative, competitive behaviour

findings.antecedent: tendencies that promote prejudice towards non-human nature
findings.consequent: prejudice towards numerous other out-groups
findings.mechanism: Underlying mechanisms of prejudice are generalizable across different out-groups.
findings.quote: the tendencies that promote prejudice towards non-human nature probably span numerous other out-groups

findings.antecedent: maladaptive responses to fear and threats
findings.consequent: problematic social behaviours, such as aggression or victimisation of out-groups
findings.mechanism: Maladaptive coping mechanisms can lead to externalized aggression and social conflict.
findings.source: text, p.73 (Greenberg et al., 2004; Stephan & Stephan, 2000)
findings.quote: maladaptive responses to fear and threats not only create a tendency towards problematic environmental behaviour, but also towards a number of other problematic social behaviours, such as aggression or victimisation of out-groups

findings.consequent: cognitively and psychologically susceptible to advertising (do not understand intent to sell, accept claims at face value)
findings.mechanism: Children's undeveloped cognitive skills make them vulnerable to persuasive advertising techniques.
findings.quote: young children are cognitively and psychologically susceptible to advertising – they typically do not understand the notion of intent to sell, and frequently accept advertising claims at face value

findings.consequent: increases children's scores on assessments of materialistic values
findings.mechanism: Media exposure acts as social modeling, promoting materialistic values.
findings.quote: exposure to commercial television increases children's scores on assessments of materialistic values

findings.consequent: contributes to alcohol and cigarette use, eating disorders, violence and sexual promiscuity
findings.mechanism: Marketing messages promote values and behaviors that can lead to various social problems.
findings.quote: exposure to marketing messages is also known to contribute to a host of other problems for young people, including alcohol and cigarette use, eating disorders, violence and sexual promiscuity

stimuli.description: short essays about their own death or about a neutral topic
pictures of wild animals being harmed (e.g., a seal caught in a fishing net)
text about recycling framed as relevant to materialistic goal of saving money or intrinsic goal of benefiting the community
lists of words typically associated with humans (e.g. wife, civilian) or with animals (e.g. wildlife, creature) presented with British or foreign names

tables.description: Circumplex model of values, based upon a study examining how 1,800 students from 15 nations rated the importance of a variety of life goals
Summary of identity-based campaign strategies for environmental challenges

limitations: Mainstream environmentalism's focus on economic benefits and 'simple and painless' changes may inadvertently reinforce materialistic values and problematic coping strategies.

Environmental organizations sometimes inadvertently exacerbate in-group/out-group distinctions between humans and nature, for example, by dismissing animal welfare concerns or framing nature instrumentally.

The paper notes that 'little research has been conducted' on experiential factors that promote environmental identity, particularly regarding human-nature interactions beyond human social interactions.
